speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):

subtopic: REFERENCE TO PRESS REPORT OF DEBATE ON SEPTEMBER 9
speechtext:
I wish to raise a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. The Canadian Press carried a dispatch dealing with the debate on Saturday, the opening paragraph of which reads as follows:
The Commons spent three hours Saturday debating an opposition motion aimed at killing a government bill seeking wide stand-by powers of control over
essential ' materials needed in Canada's rearmament program.

maintopic: ESSENTIAL MATERIALS
subtopic: REFERENCE TO PRESS REPORT OF DEBATE ON SEPTEMBER 9
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
maintopic: ESSENTIAL MATERIALS
subtopic: REFERENCE TO PRESS REPORT OF DEBATE ON SEPTEMBER 9
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: ESSENTIAL MATERIALS
subtopic: REFERENCE TO PRESS REPORT OF DEBATE ON SEPTEMBER 9
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the interjections at this point merely indicate the necessity for correcting the inaccurate impression contained in the report.

maintopic: ESSENTIAL MATERIALS
subtopic: REFERENCE TO PRESS REPORT OF DEBATE ON SEPTEMBER 9
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
maintopic: ESSENTIAL MATERIALS
subtopic: REFERENCE TO PRESS REPORT OF DEBATE ON SEPTEMBER 9
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: ESSENTIAL MATERIALS
subtopic: REFERENCE TO PRESS REPORT OF DEBATE ON SEPTEMBER 9
speechtext:
With the customary reliability of the Canadian Press, the report went on to interpret accurately the effect of the motion, and to quote certain statements that were made. There is no occasion to be critical of an interpretation which seeks to explain a motion of this kind. Hon. members of the house know, however, that a motion of this kind seeks to impress the government with the necessity for holding the bill back, revising it and presenting it in a form that is consistent with the recommendations that are made.
In view of what was said in the opening paragraph of this report, I should like to quote briefly what I said on Saturday, September 9, as reported at page 519 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, I propose to deal with two points that have been raised in the amendment that is before you. First, however, I wish to refer to the general purposes of the bill. On second reading we
532	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry are considering the principle of the bill; and basically the principle is to give to the government certain extremely broad powers for the purpose of meeting any situation which may affect our economy as the result of our defence preparations.
From the day that this house began to discuss the international situation and the steps that were being taken or not being taken to deal with it. we have sought to emphasize the fact that there is an emergency on a scale which has not been accepted or recognized by the government in any statement that has been made in this house.
Then I referred to certain details, and following reference to those details I said:
As I said yesterday, when the resolution was before us, the desire of every hon. member should be to ensure in every way he can that while we give such clearly-stated powers as can be shown to be necessary to the government, we do not abdicate our functions as members of the supreme authority of the people of Canada, and as a parliament we do not give a blank cheque to this or to any other government.
I would simply point out, Mr. Speaker, that this is a form of motion which has been accepted on a number of occasions by this government and many other governments under a similar constitution; and following that acceptance they have decided that the bill would not be read at that particular point but could be revised and brought forward in a form which would be in keeping with the recommendations which had been made. We have put forward recommendations as to the way in which this bill would carry out the intention and the purpose in a manner consistent with our constitution; and that was the purpose of the motion.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Saturday, September 9, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe for the second reading of Bill No. 5, respecting materials and services essential for the purposes of defence and national security.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION AND USE OF ESSENTIAL MATERIALS AND SERVICES
speechtext: Question.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION AND USE OF ESSENTIAL MATERIALS AND SERVICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION AND USE OF ESSENTIAL MATERIALS AND SERVICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I believe I adjourned the debate, if I am not mistaken.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION AND USE OF ESSENTIAL MATERIALS AND SERVICES
speechtext: I thought the minister was not rising.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION AND USE OF ESSENTIAL MATERIALS AND SERVICES
speechtext: I am not as fast on my feet as my hon. friend. Mr. Speaker, I wish to say just a few words about the amendment offered by the Conservative opposition to the bill now being considered by the house. I was interested in the statement of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) that the Canadian Press are quite mistaken in saying that the opposition amendment would kill the bill. Should this amendment be adopted, it would not only kill the bill but would kill the government.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION AND USE OF ESSENTIAL MATERIALS AND SERVICES
speechtext: What a blessing that would be!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION AND USE OF ESSENTIAL MATERIALS AND SERVICES
speechtext: That is a blessing to Canada that we cannot quite hope for yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION AND USE OF ESSENTIAL MATERIALS AND SERVICES
speechtext: I suggest that the Canadian Press need not apologize or bother to publish the statement of the leader of the opposition to the effect that his amendment would not kill the bill, because it would of course have exactly that effect.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION AND USE OF ESSENTIAL MATERIALS AND SERVICES
speechtext: You are not going to control the press in this bill, are you?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION AND USE OF ESSENTIAL MATERIALS AND SERVICES
speechtext:
I must say that I am amazed at the direction that the debate on this bill has taken. The bill provides for the allocation of such materials in scarce supply as may be required for the defence of Canada, and for the fixing of prices of materials so allocated, in order that the short supply may not have the effect of increasing prices.
The amendment contains parts facing in two opposite directions. First it says that the government should declare a state of emergency. There could be only one reason for that, namely, an emergency arising out of apprehended war. It would mean invoking the War Measures Act of 1914. That act

would give the government overriding power over provincial jurisdiction and allow it to take any action that in its wisdom it believed to be necessary for the prosecution of government in a state of emergency.
The amendment goes on to say that the government is taking far too wide powers. It suggests that if we wish to allocate materials we should declare in the bill the materials that we wish to allocate; that if we wish to decide what materials are in short supply, we should decide that now; that if we make an error as to the material that may in future become in short supply, there is nothing we could do about it later.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION AND USE OF ESSENTIAL MATERIALS AND SERVICES
speechtext: Nonsense.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION AND USE OF ESSENTIAL MATERIALS AND SERVICES
speechtext:
The amendment leaves the Conservative opposition in a position to go before the Canadian Corps Association and say: We want to place legislation on the statute books, and we do not want to place any limitation on the powers of the government; we want to invoke the War Measures Act and place the government in a position to do anything required. They could go before the Canadian Manufacturers Association and say: We tried to stop this clubbing of industry into submission-I believe that is a phrase that is used by the opposition. They could say: The government should by this legislation declare what materials are to be controlled, and put them under controls now, so that industry would know where it stands. That is the effect of the amendment.
Some strange phrases are being used. The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker) used the stock phrase: "Parliament is being by-passed and ignored." To show the extent to which parliament is being bynpassed and ignored, I would point out to him that in the last twelve months parliament has been in session in the months of September, October, November, January, February, March, April, May, June and August. In other words it has been in session ten out of the last twelve months-and he says that parliament is being ignored.
I believe the hon. member brought in his other phrase, namely, that we were invading fundamental freedoms and human rights in taking power to allocate materials and fix prices.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION AND USE OF ESSENTIAL MATERIALS AND SERVICES
speechtext: I never made any such statement or suggestion.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION AND USE OF ESSENTIAL MATERIALS AND SERVICES
speechtext: I thought the hon. member did.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION AND USE OF ESSENTIAL MATERIALS AND SERVICES
speechtext: Read it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION AND USE OF ESSENTIAL MATERIALS AND SERVICES
speechtext:
I thought I could find that in the hon. member's remarks. If he did not include it, I am very glad.
Essential Materials (Defence) Act

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION AND USE OF ESSENTIAL MATERIALS AND SERVICES
speechtext: Read it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION AND USE OF ESSENTIAL MATERIALS AND SERVICES
speechtext:
I would have to argue that we are not exactly doing that. If we are doing it, we are doing it in a very minor way, consistent with the situation in which this country now finds itself.
It has been suggested that this bill will permit the government to take over the railways and settle a railway strike. May I say that it does not permit the government to take over anything. True, it does give the government the right to allocate railway service, provided that there is railway service. In other words, if the railways are carrying on normally, and if it is necessary to move wheat instead of something else, such as newsprint, for instance, the government can pass an order on to the railways to do so. But there is certainly nothing in this bill that will enable the government to take over the railways, and there is nothing in the bill that will allow the government to intervene in a strike such as was dealt with by parliament in the early part of this session. If inadvertently there were such a power in the bill, the government certainly would not make use of it. Hon. members know that the government has a very different process for dealing with labour-management disputes, and there is nothing in this bill to change the process that has applied in that respect over the years.
We are told that this bill constitutes an invasion of provincial jurisdiction. The hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) went so far as to say that the bill cannot be constitutional because we had no right to invade provincial jurisdiction. I think he took all of ten minutes to study his constitutional points. I suggested his was a curbstone opinion, and he corrected me to say it was a horseback opinion. However, in this bill the government has no intention of invading provincial rights. If any order is issued which constitutes an invasion of provincial rights, the injured party has the right of appeal to the courts, and the Supreme Court of Canada will be quick to abrogate an order if it is in fact an invasion of provincial rights.
The government is advised by its Minister of Justice and is bound to accept the opinion of the Department of Justice-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION AND USE OF ESSENTIAL MATERIALS AND SERVICES
speechtext: Oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION AND USE OF ESSENTIAL MATERIALS AND SERVICES
speechtext:
-that this bill is constitutional. The government has the right to bring in measures directed toward the defence of Canada; it also has the right to enact measures relating solely to trade and commerce in this country. The government for the present

Essential Materials (Defence) Act is quite satisfied with that limited right, and feels that no additional rights are justified by the defence situation at this time.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION AND USE OF ESSENTIAL MATERIALS AND SERVICES
speechtext: What does the minister mean by "no additional rights are justified"?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION AND USE OF ESSENTIAL MATERIALS AND SERVICES
speechtext:
No rights of invading provincial jurisdiction.
We find the Conservative opposition demanding great war activity. We find them insisting that the manpower devoted to war should be expanded tremendously. We have the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) advocating that the young manpower of this country be conscripted forthwith, and yet we find-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION AND USE OF ESSENTIAL MATERIALS AND SERVICES
speechtext: On a question of privilege, the minister will not find that statement anywhere, nor can he read that interpretation into my statement, except by a complete twisting of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION AND USE OF ESSENTIAL MATERIALS AND SERVICES

Mr. Speaker, like the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) I have very little to say. I have been much interested in his remarks, and I have also been much interested in seeing him appear, among other things, as a legal authority. After all, the minister is a man of many devices and of many qualities. I suppose we should be very glad to see him appear in a new role, and I am sure the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) will be particularly glad.
The minister began by saying that this is a bill for the allocation of materials. I should like to read one or two very brief sections of the bill and then ask any reasonable and reasoning man if he can reconcile what the minister has said with the two or three brief sentences I shall read. We find this:
The minister may by order . . . prescribe the quantities of, the manner and circumstances in which and the conditions on which any essential materials may be produced, processed, used, acquired or disposed of-
And "essential materials" are defined as such materials and substances as are designated from time to time by the governor in council. So, without reading any more, I think anyone who wishes to know what the bill means will see at once that the powers are really quite extraordinary.
The minister has said, and perfectly properly, that we have been very insistent in demanding action. I would like to add that we are reasonable people, and I think we have made it clear that we wish the minister to have adequate power. But as a matter of

fact it has become fashionable in the house to do nothing about suggestions from the opposition and to give no consideration to them. If this house wished, I have very little doubt that parliament could agree on the materials which are essential and we could get away from this omnibus legislation. But as I say, we have now reached the stage in the House of Commons when an amendment is scarcely listened to; the government just plows ahead with its overwhelming majority. Even a person with my small parliamentary experience can see the difference between this parliament and the last one.
Now, I say again that I think we would say sincerely that the minister should have special powers-and also, may I add, that I think the minister would use them well. But there is such a thing as having adequate powers, and also such a thing as having unlimited powers. This bill to all intents and purposes gives unlimited powers.
There is such a thing as fighting for our way of life. We use the word "freedom" in connection with it in such a way as to lose it. Of course our amendment could easily be accepted if there were a disposition to discuss those things in a reasonable way. There are only two obstacles to its being accepted; one of them is that it is so much easier to ask for unlimited powers than to define what is needed, and the other is that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has an enormous appetite for power.
The minister is here asking for unlimited powers. Instead of his being content with what has been suggested this morning, we find that he has here what might be described as the "new look" in powers. If I recall aright, he has said this morning that he is not going to use all these powers, and that they would be safe in his hands. What he is offering here is really an "or else" proposition- "You do this, or else". I believe the members of this House of Commons, and also the people throughout the country, do not like this "or else" argument. We know that it is an argument that has flourished. It flourished in Germany under the nazis, and it flourishes in Russia today.
Do not let us fool ourselves. This bill contains a threat and an argument that if you do not do this, all kinds of things will happen. The minister is using this "or else" argument, and has told us he wants these powers and proposes to use them. I think myself it is a shocking argument to be put forward in any free assembly.
There is one other thing I would like to say, that of course the political appeal in a thing of this kind is tremendous. Let us remember that the minister has-and one might say this without exaggeration-the economy of
Essential Materials (Defence) Act Canada in the hollow of his hand. There will be all kinds of direct government contracts, and there will be indirect contracts based upon these contracts. The number of people who will be really depending upon the minister and the government, in their business life, is something which must be considered seriously. I am not hoping to impress the people in this House of Commons, but rather the people of Canada. One can imagine the minister saying to himself, "With this power I can make our party virtually impregnable."
Then we must recall this power does not go to the minister alone. It goes on to satellites, the smaller and smaller people, all depending upon powers derived by the minister, powers to invade business and to interfere with it. In fact it is not an exaggeration to say that there are endless influences the people will feel while this legislation is on the statute book, and they will feel that whatever they get in the end comes to them "with the compliments of the Minister of Trade and Commerce".
There is a disposition in some quarters to suggest that because there is a provision in section 9 requiring that these orders be tabled, parliament will in some manner control. I hope we shall not fall into any process of self-deception as stupid as that.
The minister indicated this morning that parliament was not being by-passed, because parliament would be sitting most months of the year. I do not care if parliament sits three times a day every day in the year; the powers the minister is being given here give him authority to go ahead. Tell me how, after these powers are used, when an order is tabled days, weeks or a year after, we can go back and unscramble what has been done. Let us be fair with ourselves; let us be honest with ourselves. Indeed, not only is parliament by-passed, but as a matter of fact I wonder if the cabinet is not by-passed, when wp see that many of these powers are exercisable by the minister alone.

The measure before the
house at the present time is exceedingly important. We have been dealing with matters of first importance during this session; in fact, I think it can be said that the measures which have confronted this present session of parliament are in general much more important than those that ever fell to the lot of an ordinary session of parliament in peacetime to consider. It seems to me that the measure with which the house is now called upon to deal in principle is certainly not the least important of the measures that the house has been called upon to deal with at this session. In the way in which it can touch the economic lives of the people of Canada it may in some

respects prove to be the most important measure that the house will be called upon to deal with at this special session.
Having regard to the importance of a measure of this kind, one is not unmindful of the willingness of the people of Canada to sacrifice for freedom; one is not unmindful of the need to proceed with speed to deal with emergent problems; one is certainly not unmindful of the plight faced today by many Canadian families as a result of the soaring cost of living and the fact that our defence preparations are going to be infinitely more costly than any defence preparations of a similar extent in our previous history.
Taking account of these circumstances, we as members of parliament have a fundamental duty that we owe to this institution and to the people of Canada. Emergencies will come and emergencies will go, but this parliamentary institution must go on. There must be no diminution of its position. There must be no whittling away; certainly there must be no chopping away at the foundation of our parliamentary system in meeting national problems.
I listened with a measure of interest to the remarks this morning of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) in connection with this bill and the amendment introduced on behalf of the official opposition by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). I should have thought that if this is such an emergency measure as the minister pictured it, it would have required something less than the intemperate language in which the minister indulged to support the measure. I cannot find any reason for his intemperate statement. I think the minister has demonstrated quite clearly by his touchiness that he realizes there is a great deal more in this bill, a great deal more power being given to him and the government in this bill than the house has hitherto been led to understand.
In dealing with this subject of a national emergency I do not intend to discuss the treatment of the legal aspects of that subject by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I may have something to say about the treatment of that subject by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) in his speech last Saturday. I wish, however, to say several things on the subject of the emergency.
The first is that in order to give parliament power to enact a measure of this kind there must in fact exist a national emergency. If the argument of the Minister of Justice as delivered: in this house on Saturday is that parliament in normal times, quite apart from the existence of a national emergency, possesses power to pass legislation in the form

before us, then may I say with the greatest respect that I disagree completely with him.
I doubt very much if the minister can adduce constitutional authority in support of a proposition of that kind that will very much impress the house. The fact of the matter is that there is nothing in section 91 of the British North America Act that gives parliament the right to enact legislation in sweeping terms such as these. Therefore I say there must exist a national emergency if parliament is to possess the power to deal with this situation.
I scanned the terms of this bill, particularly the recitals, for some clear statement that a national emergency does exist in order to qualify parliament to enact this measure, but I have searched in vain. There is no statement in this measure that a national emergency exists. If this bill and its constitutionality are to be founded upon the existence of a national emergency, not only is it desirable, it is essential that parliament should state in plain categorical terms its opinion that a national emergency does in fact exist.
The courts, particularly the privy council, have in direct decisions on this matter stated that if a national emergency does exist the courts will not too closely scrutinize a statement by parliament that a national emergency does exist. But there must be somewhere on the part of parliament a clear expression that it is its view that a national emergency does exist. Otherwise the courts are not going to assume that view on the part of parliament. If it is the view of the government that a national emergency does exist, and if that is the view of parliament, why should there be hesitation on the part of either the government or parliament in stating that in clear terms?
I am sick and tired of seeing the government trying to have it both ways on this subject. We have been in session now for two weeks, and I am sure it will be a matter of interest to those who in years to come read Hansard for this session to find such a cacophony of statements on the part of ministers on	this subject of national
emergency. One must wonder, after listening to their statements in their infinite variety, whether or not a national emergency exists in the view of the government.
I remember the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) a week ago Friday in which he dwelt in serious terms on the danger that may confront this nation within the next ten months. That sounded as though the Prime Minister considers there is a national emergency today. But then one listened for some days last week to the
Essential Materials (Defence) Act Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), and I defy any member of the house, after listening to the Minister of National Defence, to say that in his opinion the minister was arguing that there is a national emergency in existence today. No; the attitude of the Minister of National Defence was: Well, we are taking these problems as we come to them. We are meeting everything in our stride. Everything is all right. We have not any very definite plan, but that is the beauty of the way we go about these things. We have no plans and therefore there is no misplanning. Everything is to be dealt with as it arises. It is a sort of fluid preparation for situations that may or may not occur. No; one cannot treat anything that the Minister of National Defence said last week as reflecting a view on his part that a national emergency does in fact exist.
Then there was the speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) on Thursday evening of last week. Of course the ingrained habits of the government cannot quickly be cast off, and we had a statement, of the kind we are so accustomed to from the optimistic gentlemen who occupy the treasury benches, that everything is all right, the Canadian economy is fundamentally sound, we are at the highest peak of prosperity, everybody's pockets are full of money, and all that nonsense.
Of course it was not to be expected that the Minister of Trade and Commerce would be far behind in airy talk of that kind. In his speech when he introduced this measure at the resolution stage, if you please, he gets up and reminds the country again of the fundamental soundness of the Canadian economy. Everybody is working, everybody is happy, everything is right with the economy.
Now, sir, is there a national emergency, or is there not? If there is a national emergency, let the government have the courage and intestinal fortitude to stand up and say so. Let it demonstrate its courage by going further and inviting parliament to declare in legislative form the existence at this moment of a national emergency. Why not? If it exists, then such a declaration is necessary in order to give parliament clear power to legislate on the basis of the existence of a national emergency, and it might have a very useful and beneficial effect in many quarters. But the government has not done so. Its failure and omission to do so are, I think, not without significance. I am prepared to say categorically, Mr. Speaker, that, unless the government is prepared to say that a national emergency exists today, unless it is prepared to invite parliament so to declare, parliament

On the other hand, if an emergency does exist, then let parliament so declare. We shall know then on what basis parliament ought to be approaching the problems confronting it at this present important session. I am not of a suspicious turn of mind, but I have something more than a passing hunch why the government is falling significantly short of inviting parliament to declare that a national emergency in fact exists. I think the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) was not too discreet on Saturday in venturing some comments about the War Measures Act. I put it to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the house that the reason the government shrinks from inviting parliament to declare that a national emergency exists today is that they are afraid of the political effects in this country of creating a legislative situation where the War Measures Act may be in effect.

I invite those who believe in parliament as an institution to examine the terms of the bill. It is a matter of profound regret and disappointment that throughout this session there has been such complete silence on the part of government supporters. With scant exception, the talk on the government side has all come from cabinet ministers. If private members who support the government believe that this is the kind of legislation parliament should enact, I wish they would stand up and say so. Let them not sit back as silent men. Let them appreciate their responsibilities as members of the house and stand up and give their opinions on the bill. For one, I shall respect their frank and sincere opinions, whether or not they happen to agree with mine; but let them not sit back. Let them stand up and state those opinions, if opinions there be.
In approaching this important Bill No. 5, one who reads it cannot fail to be impressed by the absolutely sweeping character of the powers that it proposes to confer upon the governor in council. The Minister of Trade and Commerce can argue all day in the same fashion as he did this morning in attempting to convince the house that there is not very much in this bill after all, and inferentially, that even if there is, we should trust the government. They do not exceed powers- no, not they! But, sir, let the members of this house frankly and carefully examine the terms of this legislation. Let them see, in the first place, that there is no effective limitation on either the goods or the services to which the governor in council may apply his powers. We are simply legislating in the dark if we pass this measure in its present form. We are simply handing this government a blank cheque to say, in the first place, to what goods and services the power shall be applied, and in the second place, to what extent those sweeping powers shall be exercised. Let no member of this house come to vote on this subject simply having heard the soothing, syrupy statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, without having read for himself the language of this bill. Let him see that we are in effect putting dictatorial powers back into the hands of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I defy any hon. member of this house to stand up and disprove that statement.
This bill, if this house passes it and it is passed by the other place, will vest in the Minister of Trade and Commerce almost unlimited powers. He will become again, as he was in the past, the complete dictator of the Canadian economy.

It would not matter much to me if it were the member for Springfield (Mr. Sinnott) or the Minister of Trade and Commerce; either two-job John or fifty-job C.D.
Look at the powers in this bill. I invite hon. members to read the terms of sections 3 and 4. Note that those sections contain the kernel of the bill. By these sections the governor in council will acquire the power to designate from time to time as essential materials such materials or substances as in his opinion are essential for defence purposes, and to designate as essential services the carrying on of such commercial activities, including the generating and distribution of electrical energy, as in his opinion are essential for the adequate production, storage or distribution of essential materials or otherwise for defence purposes.
As if that were not enough, look at the way we find the powers extended by section 4:
The governor in council may do and authorize such acts and things and make from time to time such orders and regulations as he deems necessary for the purposes of this act to control and regulate the production, processing, distribution, acquisition, disposition or use of essential materials or the supply or use of essential services.
Then there follows the enumeration of the things he may do if he deems it necessary:
(a)	require any person who produces, processes, deals in or has in his possession or control any essential materials to deal with, supply or dispose of any such materials in such manner and in such priority to that person's other transactions as the minister may prescribe;
(b)	require any person who produces or processes any essential materials to produce or process any such materials in such manner and in such priority to that person's other production or processing operations as the minister may prescribe;
(c)	prescribe the quantities of, the manner and circumstances in which and the conditions on which any essential material may be produced, processed, used, acquired or disposed of, . . .
Essential Materials (Defence) Act
(d)	require any person who supplies any essential service to supply the service to such persons, to such extent and on such conditions as the minister may prescribe;
(e)	prescribe the restrictions and conditions according to which an essential service may be supplied or used, either generally or within periods of time prescribed by the minister, and for these purposes may require persons to obtain permits;
(f)	fix the maximum prices, either by determining the selling price or the mark-up, at which and the terms and conditions on which any essential materials or essential services may be sold or offered for sale by any person; and require any seller to refund to any buyer any sum or consideration received in excess of a maximum selling price so fixed.
These are only a few of the powers, Mr. Speaker. There is no time at this stage to read the whole list. Can any member reading those provisions of the bill deny that if the minister is given powers as sweeping as those, he holds the economy of this country in the hollow of his hand? We of the Progressive Conservative opposition have said that if the government will plainly state the extent of the emergency we are quite prepared that clearly defined powers should be legislated in proper parliamentary form to meet the emergency according to the extent that it exists. But we are not prepared simply to abdicate our functions as members of the House of Commons of Canada and hand over all these powers nor to abdicate in favour of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I ask hon. members to go further and to examine the recitals in this bill. Bear in mind, sir, that the only possible constitutional justification for parliament to proceed to deal with measures of this kind is the existence of a national emergency-not in the .future, but today. It would be completely unconstitutional for parliament to say: In case a national emergency should arise some time in the next six months we now give powers to the government which will come into effect if and when a national emergency arises. Such a course would be illegal. It would be utterly unconstitutional. Yet I say to you, sir, that is precisely what this bill purports to do.
Look at the recitals. I have already indicated that we do not find there the slightest trace of a clear statement that a national emergency exists today. You will find in the fourth paragraph of the preamble a statement that steel and other materials, electrical energy, may be insufficient-it does not say that they are-to meet the requirements. In the final paragraph of this preamble it is said:
... in order to avert possible disruption of such defence preparations, to lessen the resultant disruption of normal trade and commerce and to prevent economic disorder and hardship on a national scale it is essential in the interest of Canada as a whole

Essential Materials (Defence) Act to provide for the control and regulation of the production, distribution and use of such materials and services.
But, sir, what dues the Minister of Trade and Commerce say while putting that recital in the mouth of parliament? He says we are not going to exercise these powers today; we are simply taking stand-by powers so that if a national emergency does arise we shall have the power to act. I say to you that between the statements of the minister and these recitals in the bill there is a complete contradiction. When parliament is toeing asked to legislate in the terms of this bill in the face of a statement of the kind we have heard from the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I say to you that parliament is toeing called upon to legislate fundamental dishonesty. If the Minister of Trade and Commerce was correct, then the terms of this preamble are wrong, and parliament has no right to legislate in those terms. It is absolutely destructive of what is fundamental in the constitution of this country for parliament to say today we are going to create powers to come into effect if and when a national emergency arises, but we are not saying a national emergency exists today. I say to this house, that if the majority of the members want to vest in the Minister of Trade and Commerce these dictatorial powers and want to make them stick in a legal sense, it is necessary to say that a national emergency does exist which requires parliament to confide such sweeping powers in the minister.
But that has not been said. The government have not had the courage to say it. What they are calling upon parliament to do in this lame way is to say that if a national emergency arises some time before parliament meets again, then parliament will have this power by reason of a national emergency, even though we are not saying that one exists today. That, Mr. Speaker, is fundamental dishonesty in legislation.
When the privy council laid down the principle that in a national emergency parliament would have the right to encroach upon fields of jurisdiction that normally are assigned to the provincial legislatures by the division of constitutional power in this country under the British North America Act, I certainly do not think they ever intended that parliament should abdicate the right and duty to declare the existence of a national emergency, and place it, as would be done by this bill, in the hands of the governor in council-which means in the hands of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, in effect-to declare the existence of a national emergency, thereby and 

at that time effecting a transfer to the Minister of Trade and Commerce of wide constitutional powers at the expense of the legislatures of the provinces.
Some hon. member may say: Oh, the emergency may come swiftly; we must anticipate it. I ask him to recall the fact that a national emergency descended upon this country just two and a half weeks ago, in the form of a complete railway stoppage. On that occasion the government called parliament. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that parliament can be called to deal with any national emergency that exists requiring the use of powers in excess of those that we in our amendment have indicated we are prepared to see conferred to the extent of any present emergency that the government is prepared to show exists, provided that those powers are clearly defined in the act and are not made an occasion for abdication on the part of parliament in favour of a minister of the crown.
Parliament can meet in a hurry. This idea that parliament is not capable of meeting the exigencies of a national emergency in haste has gone forever. The Royal Canadian Air Force, Trans-Canada Air Lines and the other means that were resorted to in order to bring members of parliament to Ottawa in haste have effectively disposed of that bogey which has served the political interests of this government extremely well, to their satisfaction in times past.
I invite hon. members to consider calmly and dispassionately the amendment which has been put forward on behalf of the official opposition by the hon. member for Lake Centre, and to have due regard to the actuality of the extent of the power proposed under this bill to be confided in the governor in council.
Our amendment reads as follows:
That Bill No. 5 be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that while this house is ready and anxious to adopt all appropriate measures which will prevent economic hardship and disorder on a national scale and provide for the necessary regulation of the production, distribution and use of materials and services for defence purposes, it regrets the circumstances connected with the introduction and prosecution of this measure, namely, that the government has failed to name and declare the national emergency upon which it seeks to base authority for this bill and has not specified the materials and services which are to be subject to the provisions of the bill.
If the government wanted to do it, Mr. Speaker, it would be relatively simple to spell out the necessary goods and services that are required to be provided for now, in the light of defence preparations. The house has only to look at Bill No. 4-and I am not going to discuss that bill at the

moment. I use it merely as an illustration of the way in which, when the government wishes to and when this house requires it, the things to which the powers are to extend can be defined. I am not altogether satisfied with the provisions of Bill No. 4 in that respect. But at least Bill No. 4 contains an answer to those who are saying that there is no other way of doing this thing, that you cannot spell out the necessary powers that are required to meet the situation, that you cannot specify the goods and services that ought to be designated as those to which the powers will apply; it is an answer to those who say that you simply have to hand over holus-bolus, to an omnipotent minister of the crown, everything in the way of power. In its own Bill No. 4 the government has given the answer to that kind of argument.

I have listened, Mr. Speaker, with considerable interest and attention to the arguments that have been put forward by members of the Progressive Conservative
Essential Materials (Defence) Act party with reference to the constitutional and parliamentary aspects of this whole matter. I take second place to no one in concern for the responsibility to parliament of the government of this country. I take second place to no one in insisting that parliament must know at all times the full meaning of the legislation that it passes, particularly when that legislation gives powers to the government. In that connection, we have already made it plain that we want a clear-cut statement from the minister as to what this bill means and as to what it may not mean. That indeed was the import of the question asked a while ago by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), who said that he would answer the question when he closed the debate on the main motion.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION AND USE OF ESSENTIAL MATERIALS AND SERVICES
speechtext:
I am asking the minister not to forget his promise to speak about that matter when he closes the debate on the main motion.
I was about to say, however, that I am fully prepared to give to my hon. friends to the right-the Progressive Conservatives- full marks for their interest in the constitutional aspects of this question and for their interest in maintaining the control of parliament over the government. At the same time I cannot help but wonder if some of the vehemence of their opposition to this bill does not stem also from the fact that they in principle do not like to see business and industry-as they sometimes put it-"pushed around by the government".
The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) says that "regulated" would be a better word, and I agree. But the other phrase expresses the feelings of those opposed to any such regulation, and that is why I used it.
Our position in this matter, Mr. Speaker, is very clear. We supported controls on our economy in the interests of the people during world war II. And we urged that those controls, particularly where they were clearly necessary, should be continued in the period of peace that followed world war II. Accordingly, when we now ask for the reimposition of price controls, which we think were wrongfully and -too hastily removed, it is a continuation of the policy that we have advocated right through the years.
May I make it clear that during the years of peace, when we asked for the continuance or the reimposition of price controls, we took the position that in our view it was within

Essential Materials (Defence) Act the constitutional power of the federal parliament to take that course. The former member for Kindersley, Mr. Frank Jaenicke, went into that from the legal point of view on a number of occasions, and cited in particular the decision of the privy council in the Canada Temperance Act case, where words were used to the effect that whenever a matter by its inherent nature is of concern or importance to the whole country the federal parliament has the right to deal with it.
We contended through the years, even when there was no War Measures Act in effect, that on the basis of that decision, because the matter of prices, by its inherent nature, was of concern and of importance to the people of Canada from coast to coast, this parliament had the right to legislate in the field of price controls.
As to the argument my friends to the right are making about the necessity of the government declaring an emergency before they can go into this field, I for one do not think such a course has to be taken. I think the decision to which I have already referred, and which we quoted a number of times during the years since the end of world war II, is sufficient basis for the federal parliament acting in this matter in the interests of all the people of Canada.
I confess that I am going to have a few words to say about constitutional matters myself, Mr. Speaker, but I want to urge that the important question before this parliament, the question the people of Canada are now asking, is what the government's position is going to be in this matter. And while I would hope that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) might pay some attention to the arguments that I am going to make respecting the constitutional aspects of the matter, I am most anxious that the Minister of Trade and Commerce should make a clear-cut statement on this matter in reply to the questions which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar put to him, because it is very clear from the way prices are rising, the way they are getting out of hand, that nothing is of so much concern to our people in this country today, certainly on the home front, as the need for this government to take steps to protect the living standards of our own people.
With respect to the discussion that has taken place on the constitutional aspects I should like to say this. I respect, as all of us do, the constitution of this country. One must do so if he believes, as I do, in the rule of law. It should not be treated disrespectfully. At the same time we think it should be improved. The constitution itself should be brought up to date; it should be made to meet


the conditions of 1950 rather than the conditions of 1867. But what I do not like about the way in which this government treats the constitution is that they trot it out as an excuse for not doing something when they do not want to follow a certain course, but they drive a twenty-mule team through it when there is something that they decide they want to do. Look at what has happened in this very session. When we have been pressing for the reimposition of price controls the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has said to us that they have talked the matter over and have come to the conclusion that it would be an invasion of provincial rights to go into that field. In other words, it would be in violation of the constitution; and the urgent request of the people of Canada for price controls is denied because of the constitution. But when the government decides that they want the particular kind of powers which are set out in the bill now before us, which include the power to control the prices of certain commodities and services, the Minister of Justice rises in his place and says that the federal parliament has the right to do that under the headings of national defence and trade and commerce, as set out in section 91 of the British North America Act.
I would like the Minister of Justice to explain to me how it is that control over trade and commerce gives the federal authority the right to control prices of steel and electricity, but does not give it the power to control the price of bread, which has been going up in a concerted fashion across this country lately.
It seems to me that we had a similar disregard of the constitution when the government brought in the bill respecting instalment buying. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) admitted that that control was in effect during the war under the War Measures Act. But the Minister of Finance said he was bringing that measure in now under the responsibility of the federal parliament for currency and credit. When I heard the minister use that phrase it registered something in my mind that made me wonder about it, and so I thought I had better look it up in the British North America Act. I found that section 91 of the British North America Act does not say that the parliament of Canada has control over currency and credit, but rather class 14 of section 91 reads: "Currency and coinage."
The Minister of Finance said that the purpose of that bill was to do something about inflation. I do not think he needed to quote that section of the British North America Act, either correctly or incorrectly. I think he was perfectly within his rights in saying this problem of inflation, by its inherent nature, is of concern and of importance to the whole

people of Canada, and on that basis they had the right to bring in that bill. Whether or not we agree with it is another question. That is my view with respect to this whole question of the constitution. I think the government is bringing the constitution into disrespect by proceeding in this way, by the Prime Minister saying on the one hand we cannot give you price controls because it is unconstitutional, and on the other hand by the government bringing in a bill that provides for such price controls as the Minister of Trade and Commerce thinks are good, the indications so far being that only such items as steel and electricity are in mind.
Well, now, they cannot have it both ways. I am not seeking to buttress the arguments of my hon. friends to the right, that it is necessary to declare an emergency. I have already said that we did not think it was necessary in 1947, 1948 and 1949, when we were asking for the control of prices in peacetime. But I do think that the government should stop this driving of a team of horses through the constitution the way they have been doing, and using it in both ways, as has been the case in this very session.
Our position is clear. Our quarrel with this bill is not that it does not declare an emergency, but rather that it does not go far enough in the field of controlling our economy in the interests of our people to meet the emergency which is already here; and along with that it does not go far enough in spelling out clearly what the powers are that the minister is taking.
I look at this bill at times and say to myself: Maybe it does give the minister power to go into the field of general price controls; but then I realize that that would have to be taken in conjunction with the context of the preamble, although Beauchesne says that preambles are not important in legislation. I suppose, too, it would have to be taken in the light of what the minister said the purpose of this bill was, and what he may still tell us is its purpose. But that being the case, we are left near the end of this important special session with no guarantee to the people of Canada that there will foe legislation to protect their living standards.
One other word and I shall resume my seat. Sometimes it is said to us that it is strange that we talk so much about freedom and at the same time talk about controls. Surely it is elemental that in order for people to have real freedom there must be economic freedom, freedom from the poverty and suffering that economic tyranny so often imposes upon our people. We are not asking for control of our people; we are asking for control
Essential Materials (Defence) Act of economic forces, control of the economic order of this country so that there may be a chance for economic freedom for our people.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND REGULATION OF PRODUCTION, DISTRIBUTION AND USE OF ESSENTIAL MATERIALS AND SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, considerable heat has been displayed in the discussion of this measure. I should like now to place before the ministry, and particularly the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), one or two suggestions with regard to this legislation which I hope will be given at least careful consideration. I hope also that as a result the government will make amendments to the bill.
In the first place I do urge most strongly that there be written into the bill, as a schedule thereto, a list of the materials and services which are to be considered as essential, and which will therefore become subject to the powers set out in the bill. It may be that there should also be power taken in the bill for the cabinet to add to that list; for the moment I am not arguing that such is the case, but the bill would be much less objectionable if a list were written into it showing what materials and services the government considers essential. If there should be a war, and a much longer list of materials became essential, that difficulty would be met by the fact that in such event the War Measures Act would be invoked at once.
Parliament will be sitting again within about four months. We need deal now only with that period of time from the middle of September until, let us say, the middle of January. It is not as though there were any great necessity to enact legislation now which would foe sufficient for a year or for a longer period of time. At this special session parliament need only provide for the next four or [DOT] five months.
In the preamble to the bill one of these materials regarded as essential is actually listed, as is also one type of essential service. I refer hon. members to the fourth paragraph in the preamble, which reads:
And whereas steel and other materials and electrical energy and other services will be urgently required for such defence preparations and it is expected that the supply of such materials and services may be insufficient to meet such requirements together with the requirements of normal trade and commerce . . .
The draftsman of the bill took the unusual course of setting out one material and one type of service which were regarded as essential. This having been done, it seems strange that we find in the bill no schedule listing all such materials and services; on the contrary, in the bill itself a general power is given to the cabinet to declare that any
544	HOUSE OF
Essential Materials (Defence) Act material or any service may be considered essential, and therefore under the provisions of the bill.
While I have not had an opportunity to check the legislation in the United States, I believe that in that country the government has stated what particular materials are to be covered by their bill. I have before me an issue of U.S. News and World Report for September 8, and at page 23 I find this:
A new government list of materials that are considered "critical at this time" offers a clue to where controls may hit first. This list, published by the general services administration, includes eleven items: aluminum, cement, copper, lead, leather, lumber, paper, rubber, steel, wool and zinc.
When the resolution preceding the bill was under discussion the other day I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce what materials he had in mind. His reply is found at page 460 of Hansard in these words:
Any item where war buying interferes with the normal civilian supply. It could easily be copper or zinc. Nickel is already being rationed by the producer in consultation with the government. It is being rationed both in Canada and the United States.
Then I asked if lumber would be included, and the minister answered:
Lumber might very well be one of these commodities.
I repeat the hope that the government will give consideration to attaching to the bill a schedule containing the materials and services which it is believed will be essential during the next four months.
Such action is not merely a question of doing what is right in drafting a bill, but is fundamentally sound for two other reasons. In the first place, these laws are drawn to control the conduct of the Canadian people, and our people are entitled to know exactly what the terms of the law are. It is unwise to have them in a state of doubt, realizing that there are general powers but not knowing in just what way those powers will apply.
The people of Canada are entitled to definite, clear-cut legislation, particularly where that legislation is punitive. This bill is of a punitive type. As the minister himself said the other day, it is to be used as a threat to the people. Where we have punitive legislation of that kind it should be clear-cut; there should be no generalities; yet this bill is not clear-cut at all. As I have said, it does not state what materials or services are to be covered, but gives very wide general powers to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I have no intention of reading them at this time, but hon. members will find them set out in section 4(2). Not only does it give those general powers to the minister; it gives them also to anyone he chooses to appoint to


carry them out. For example, we find that section 5, subsection 2, reads:
The minister may authorize persons to act under his control and direction on his behalf in the exercise of powers conferred on him by this act or by regulations.
As I read that subsection it means that an administrator or controller appointed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce could issue an order which would have the same effect as though the order had been issued by the minister. In other words, there will be no necessity for the minister to approve any such order; it can be put out by his officers. While there is provision for the publishing of regulations made by the government under sections 3, 4 and 10, there is no such provision with respect to the orders issued by the minister or one of his officials. Orders issued under section 4, subsection 2, do not have to be published in the Canada Gazette or laid before parliament. Those particular orders are the ones which should be checked most carefully, because they tell John Jones or William Smith exactly what he has to do. I repeat that there is no provision in the bill for having such orders published or laid before parliament.
The bill is not in the clear-cut terms to which the Canadian people are entitled. As I have said, it is punitive legislation; I think it can fairly be described as big-stick legislation. The Minister of Trade and Commerce explained frankly his attitude with regard to this legislation as 'reported at page 460 of Hansard of September 8. I quote:
I suggest to the committee that a word from the government is more effective if there is a law in the background that can be applied in case the response is not all that may be desired.
He had been explaining that it is possible generally to bring about satisfactory arrangements with businessmen by sitting around a table, but the minister added that he wanted this power behind him so that if Canadians would not agree to the terms imposed by the minister or his advisers, there would be a big stick that could be used. Let us not be in any doubt about it, this is big-stick legislation. Legislation of that type is fundamentally unsound. But if we are to have it, then let us have the terms written clearly into the statute so that the Canadian who is to be affected thereby may know exactly what are his obligations.
Just a word or two with regard to parliament and this type of legislation. During the last war parliament was by-passed, generally speaking, and the country was governed by order in council. I admit that such action was necessary. Time and again the opposition

refrained from criticizing government measures because we thought we might hurt Canada's war effort. It was only human nature that every member of the cabinet who served during the war years, as well as every government supporter, and perhaps every member of the opposition, lost some of the respect for parliament he had had before war commenced. Things had to be done differently under the pressure of war, and unfortunately parliament lost a great deal of its prestige and a great deal of its actual power. Parliament was one of the casualties of the last war, and we should remember that at the present time. Since 1946 we have been faced with what has been called a cold war. We are now in another era which I referred to the other night as the Korean era, and which I notice the papers are calling a warm war. We have gone from the cold war stage to the warm war stage and the publication from which I quoted a few minutes ago says that it is expected that this latter stage will last at least five years if we do not have a third world war.
No matter how long it lasts, we are certainly in for a period which can properly be known as a warm war. The government has said that this is not the time to use the War Measures Act; the ministers have been careful not to go that far, but I do suggest that in this warm war era there is a great need to maintain the prestige of parliament and the respect for parliament across the nation. If we are not careful in these days when there are such great worries we are apt to take steps which will ruin completely the usefulness of parliament in Canada. There is a far greater danger of that happening now than there was in 1939 when war broke out because of what has been going on for the last ten years.
In this bill the Canadian parliament is not being given a square deal. We are being asked to pass legislation which is punitive in character and which is not clear-cut. We are being asked to pass that legislation under pressure, and in my opinion any such step will be doing parliament great harm and will be a great injustice to the Canadian people.
In concluding may I urge upon the Prime Minister and the cabinet that they give consideration to setting out in this bill a schedule of the materials and services which are to be controlled for the next four months. In my opinion that would remove the worst feature of this legislation and go a long way toward helping parliament to maintain the respect of the Canadian people.

Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade
and Commerce): In the course of this lengthy debate, Mr. Speaker, I think that most matters have been discussed. In speaking to the amendment, however, I said that I would give more details of the bill which was recently passed by the congress of the United States and which extends to the president of that country powers somewhat similar to those referred to in the bill before us. I have not the act itself. A printed copy of it has not reached Ottawa as yet; at least, it has not reached my desk. The purposes of the act are to facilitate the production of goods and services necessary for national security through a system of priorities and allocations of materials and facilities; by providing financial assistance to expand productive capacity and supply, by strengthening controls over credit and regulating speculation on commodity exchanges.
Section 101 of the bill gives the president authority to require contracts to be accepted and performed with priority, and to allocate materials and facilities in order to promote the national defence.
Section 102 prohibits the hoarding for personal, business, or home consumption, or for the purpose of resale at greater than market prices, materials which have been designated by the president as scarce materials.

Section 103 provides for a fine up to $10,000 for failure to comply with the anti-hoarding regulations.
Section 201 gives the president authority to requisition plants and facilities, including materials, for national defence purposes and to pay for them and to return them to the owners on payment of the fair value thereof after the property is no longer required. If compensation set by the president is unacceptable, the owners can accept seventy-five per cent of the amount set, and take court action to settle the amount of compensation.
Sections 301 and 302 give the president authority to make loans, either direct or by guaranteeing private loans, for expansion to meet defence needs. The authority to supply or disburse funds for this purpose can be delegated by the president to "guaranteeing agencies"-that is, government departments or agencies such as army, commerce, et cetera, responsible for national defence procurement.
Section 303 allows for the government purchase of scarce materials including metals, minerals and liquid fuels, and for the exploration, development and mining of critical minerals and metals; and includes the right to transport, store and have materials processed and refined.
Section 304: The total amount borrowed is not to be more than $600 million outstanding at any one time. In addition, sums not exceeding $1,400 million can be appropriated to carry out sections 302 and 303.
The sections under the title of price and wage stabilization vest wages and price control authority in the president, the main exceptions being prices or rentals for real property, margin requirements on any commodity exchange, rates or fees for professional services, rates charged on any common carrier or public utility. I point out that these are excepted from the provisions of the act.
Section 401 sets out the objectives behind price and wage stabilization, for example, to prevent inflation, eliminate profiteering and hoarding, maintain balance between purchasing power and supply of consumer goods and services.
Section 402 provides the president with authority to approve voluntary programs and agreements on the part of business, agriculture, labour and consumers to stabilize prices and wages. To the extent these programs are unsuccessful, the president has the authority to initiate selective price controls which must be accompanied by wage controls within the industry producing the product subject to price rulings. If general price controls are introduced, there must also be general wage controls.

Wages are to be stabilized at rates paid during the period from May 24, 1950 to June 24, 1950, inclusive. Extensive regulations governing prices of agricultural commodities are set out in subsection (d) (3).
Section 403 provides that at such time as the president determines it is necessary to impose price and wage controls generally over a substantial portion of the national economy, he shall administer such controls and rationing at the retail level of consumer goods for household and personal use, through a new independent agency created for the purpose.
Sections 404 to 409 deal mainly with regulations governing protests against this part of the act or violations of its terms.

Now that the house
has heard the explanation by the minister, more than ever I say the criticism advanced by the opposition becomes even more tenable. The minister tells us that there is similar legislation in the United States, and he produces a summary of the legislation passed within the last two days by the United States congress. The interesting point in connection with what he has stated bears out the basis of the criticism made by the opposition, namely, that whereas in the United States the full powers being granted are written into the act to the extent of some 800 sections, as I understand it, thereby giving in detail the power granted to the president by the United States congress and limiting his powers to the legislative authority comprised in the act, we in this country are giving to the minister full and uncontrolled powers.
It was stated on Saturday that it would be possible to challenge anything that had been done in excess of the powers being conveyed to the minister in these general terms. One realizes from the experience of the past that any such challenge by way of amendment to the address in reply, or on going into committee of supply or otherwise, would be regarded as a vote of non-confidence and would be voted down. So that constitutional power which is referred to in such fulsome terms by the Minister of Justice is indeed nothing more than a sham and a delusion in this parliament.
There is no control under this bill over 'the absolute powers of the minister. On previous occasions we have given powers to the minister and he has used them under

orders in council so as to deny the rights of individuals to the rule of law. I will give one example. In an order in council passed under the general powers vested by parliament in the government during the days of war, a controller was set up. Under that order in council provision was made whereby any person brought before the controller to give evidence was refused any constitutional safeguards whatever, and refused counsel. There was a provision in that order in council whereby, however illegally the controller acted, the individual had no right of recourse.
All of us in the House of Commons wish to do everything we can to assist in the mobilization of our country for defence. What we contend for in this debate is not our opposition to the granting of necessary powers to the minister, but rather to the granting of absolute powers which permit him to deny to the individual the right of recourse to the courts and, if he wishes to do so, to deny to any individual equality under the law.
The minister mentioned a while ago that the hon, member for Lake Centre would have objected to certain provisions. There would be no objection if we had in this measure the right of the individual to appeal to the courts, a right which is given in the United States act.
Under the United States act, if the president acts in such a manner as to cause a subject of that country to believe it to be a denial of justice under the law, there is a right of recourse to the courts. Under the United States law, when the president directs an individual or a corporation to do anything -to sell, for instance, at a price designated by the president-the individual against whom such order was made has a right of recourse either to arbitration or to the courts so as to preserve his rights.
This bill in its present form simply amounts to the granting of extraordinary powers to be exercised by the minister or the governor in council without a right on the part of any person to raise objection in the courts as against any injustice that may be done. We are willing to grant rights; but our objection has been that in doing so we must preserve under the law the right of the individual to protect himself against arbitrary caprice or injustice that may be exercised by the minister or by his successor or by the governor in council.
No one objects to the giving of powers to the executive at this time, provided that we in parliament know what we are giving. It was interesting to note that the minister could not and did not give assurance in con-
Essential Materials (Defence) Act nection with bringing in a system of price controls; indeed he indicated that under this measure he would not have power to do so. As I understood him, his powers will simply be the right on his part !to intervene in connection with commodities required for defence. If an arbitrary price is asked, or scarcity results, he will then be able to step in.
But that is not what the sections mean, if they are interpreted in their ordinary terms. Those sections give to the minister absolutely uncontrolled power to do anything which in his opinion he considers necessary. The interpretation of the act will be his interpretation. The limitations upon his powers will be the limitations he chooses to put upon his powers. No individual whose rights are interfered with has any right under this measure as it now stands to do more than make an objection. The courts of this country are denied to the individual, although they are not denied under the powers conferred upon the President of the United States.	.
We believe that parliament has a right not to grant powers that depend for their interpretation upon the will of a minister. We believe that the powers granted should be set out in such a way that those who run may read. Under the measure in the United States, any person in that country can refer to the statute and there find the power granted to the president. As to the blanket powers granted under this measure, no one may know what their limitation may be. However far the minister may go in his interpretation of his powers, he alone, in his supremacy, may say that his decision is the final decision. The courts of this land have no right to delimit him in any way, or indeed to protect the subject, regardless of how unfair the order may be. He may say to one individual: You shall sell at such and such a price; and to another individual within the same industry: You shall sell at a lesser price. When provision is made whereby any minister of the crown has the power, as among individuals within a class, of extending certain rights 'to one individual that he may deny to another, no one in this house can say that such power should be granted by parliament.
We agree with the objective. We want to see everything done at this time to mobilize the nation. The Minister of Justice found something on Saturday. He found the War Measures Act, which is known to every person in this country. He gave his reasons why the government did not proceed under the War Measures Act. My answer is that the War Measures Act was not used

Essential Materials (Defence) Act because if it had been used the question of the mobilization of manpower would have to be faced. If the minister is to have the power to say to an industry what it shall produce, and to a producer what he shall produce; or if he can direct that the production of a certain commodity shall be expanded, he has to have the power as well to control and direct manpower in order to secure the production that he requires.
I repeat that if the War Measures Act had been invoked it would have been necessary to deal also with the matter of manpower, and it was for that reason that this method of dealing with the question has been used. We are given a bill which is allegedly an imitation of the bill empowering the President of the United States, but in fact it is as far removed from the bill in the United States as daylight is from darkness. In the one case the president gets power which is controlled by the courts and designated by congress; in this bill the governor in council and the minister get powers which are undefined, unexplained and uncircumscribed, and without providing for the right on the part of the individual to raise any objection. After saying that the minister shall have these tremendous powers, finally, in order that there may be no mistake, the bill provides that the minister shall be empowered to do such further things in regard to the production, supply, distribution and use of essential materials or services as may be authorized by order or regulation.
